newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians protest despite government appeal.
newsitem.headline: Albanians protest despite government appeal.

text.p: Furious Albanian investors staged more protests on Sunday, ignoring government suggestions to shrug off millions of dollars in losses from failed pyramid investment schemes and to get back to work.
Several thousand protesters marched through the southern towns of Fier and Vlore, chanting anti-government slogans and demanding compensation for losses.
In Vlore, where the Gjallica scheme went bust and wiped out the savings of many residents, about 2,000 people marched and carried the picture of a protester who was shot dead last week.
In Fier, another 2,000 people staged a protest, denouncing President Sali Berisha and carrying local opposition Socialist Party leader Petro Koci through the town on their shoulders.
"There is a war between Fieri residents and Berisha. Be assured we will win. The government says yours is an economic protest but they are wrong. It is political, too," he told the crowd.
No riot police were seen in Vlore or Fier on Sunday, part of a new strategy by the right-wing government to let marches go ahead unopposed outside the capital.
Albania has been swept by demonstrations and riots since five high-risk schemes collapsed last month. Vlore was the scene of bloody clashes last week in which three people died.

Investors blame the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi for failing to warn them of the dangers of the schemes, which said they were building tourist resorts, supermarkets and petrol stations but were, in fact, pocketing the cash.
In Tirana, police put on a show of force to ensure a rally called by the main opposition Forum for Democracy on Sunday did not take place.
A dozen police vans and cars cruised the area and officers moved quickly to make sure people kept going and did not loiter near the football stadium where the rally was due to be held.
Officers forced customers in nearby cafes out into a heavy rain storm to make sure that if any were potential protesters they would disperse or get drenched.
Berisha admitted on Saturday that it had been a mistake to use riot police against protesters and told reporters protests would be allowed in Tirana, too, if organisers had a permit.
But Sunday's actions showed the government is still loathe to let demonstrations take place in the capital and was hoping protests in the countryside would diminish.
In his first explanation of the calamity, Berisha said on Saturday the government had committed errors and had warned the public too late about the dangers of the unregulated schemes.
But he said sternly that responsibility also lay with those who had put millions of dollars into the high-interest schemes -- and lost everything.
He stressed that the state had no intention of reimbursing hundreds of thousands of Albanians who lost their savings and often sold valuables or property to invest in the schemes.
"We will not take this debt on our shoulders. No democratic government would do this. It would be cheating, printing money to pay and creating hyperinflation", he said.
Berisha acknowledged that many Albanians were now homeless, having sold houses or flats to join a frenzy of investing in the schemes which paid interest of 60 percent or more a month.
Bankers estimate $1 to $2 billion may have been poured into the fraudulent schemes. Anti-government protests and riots have swept the country since January when they began to fall.
Berisha said there was no question of early elections over the scandal and Meksi has made clear he has no intention of quitting. Meksi has taken a hard line throughout the scandal.
"At the moment the only way for Albanians to get back their money back ... is to work and be calm," he said by telephone on Saturday.
